fulfillment: The binding is too broad and the node treats the final spatial relation as sufficient proof of fulfillment. In the edited image, a mug is indeed to the right of the headphones, but the source shows the mug on their left; the edit also leaves a mug-like object on the left and introduces a conspicuous blurred blue remnant. Thus the requested move appears to have progressed, but the image does not clearly establish that the original mug was moved cleanly or that the requested edit is complete. Make the node compare the same target and reference across source and edited snapshots, and distinguish partial progress from complete fulfillment while applying the rubric; do not infer absence from the artifacts or unrelated changes. The two support observations are highly confident but appear to repeat the same final-image relation, not independently verify change or completion. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is reported, so investigate the semantic evidence and criterion application rather than execution.
s2: The binding checks only whether some visible mug is right of the headphones, so it can pass on a newly introduced mug while ignoring whether the source mug moved. Bind the comparison to the same identifiable target across source and edited snapshots, and assess its displacement relative to the headphones. Keep the spatial-relation check distinct from the fulfillment criterion: a right-side mug alone does not establish that the requested move is complete when the source mug remains on the left and a blurred blue remnant is visible. Use the rubric to distinguish demonstrated progress from completion, and leave the result unresolved if target identity or movement cannot be established; do not treat artifacts as proof of no progress. The repeated high-confidence observations support only the final-image relation, not independent evidence of change. This is a semantic binding/evidence issue, not a transport, schema, or dependency failure.
s1: The node’s evidence-availability check is appropriate as a support check, but its binding is incomplete: it considers only the edited image and can identify any mug, rather than establishing that the requested objects and their relation are observable across the source and edited snapshots. Keep this node focused on visibility/identifiability, not fulfillment; explicitly report whether the source mug can be matched to an edited mug and whether the headphones can be matched, leaving identity or comparison inconclusive when warranted. Here the source has one blue mug left of the headphones, while the edit shows a mug on the right, another mug-like object near the headphones, and a conspicuous blurred blue remnant on the left. These are evidence of ambiguity and possible progress, not proof that the original mug was cleanly moved or that no change occurred. The downstream fulfillment check should use that evidence to distinguish partial progress from completion under the rubric. Avoid treating the high-confidence final-image relation as independent evidence of movement; calibrate confidence to the cross-image identity evidence. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is reported, so the repair should target semantic binding and evidence scope.

rejected_diagnostics.semantic_rejection: The fulfillment readout is not given the source or edited images, yet its criteria require it to decide whether the original mug remains or whether the right-side mug is additional. The relocation support can report that evidence, but the fulfillment criteria do not faithfully compose its possible outcomes: they allow partial when the original mug remains or the right-side mug is additional, even though the relocation check can fail because the source mug is elsewhere and not to the right, which does not establish progress toward the requested placement. They also do not clearly map a failed relocation check with no progress to absent. Thus the readout can misclassify or leave required cases unresolved.
